# On Losing the Key to the Storage Unit

Three years of not needing it. That's how long it sat in a junk drawer before I finally lost the key to unit 214 (the one with my grandmother's china, four boxes of yearbooks, and a bicycle I keep meaning to sell). I noticed it was gone on a Sunday, looking for a spare house key, and spent twenty minutes convinced it had simply migrated to a coat pocket somewhere.

It hadn't. I checked every coat first, then every bag, then the car, twice.

The facility's front office was staffed by a guy named Dale who has apparently seen this exact problem four times a week for the eleven years he's worked there. He didn't even blink. "Lock cutters," he said, "or we drill it, your choice, either way you're paying for a new lock." The drilling option was forty dollars cheaper, so that's what I picked, mostly out of stinginess rather than any real preference.

It took him about six minutes with a cordless drill to get through a lock that had, presumably, been engineered to resist exactly that. I asked if that bothered him, professionally speaking. He shrugged and said the good locks take fifteen minutes, and if someone really wants in, they're getting in regardless of what you spend on the lock — the point of a decent lock is just to make it not worth the effort, not to make it impossible.

Inside, the unit smelled like cardboard and dust, unsurprisingly. The china was fine. The yearbooks had a faint must to them but nothing ruined. The bicycle had two flat tires and a layer of grime that came off in one long swipe when I ran a rag down the frame, which felt oddly satisfying, like proving the thing was still a bicycle and not just a shape rust was slowly becoming.

I asked Dale, while he filled out the paperwork, how often people actually come back for their units after something like this. Most of them, he said. Some don't, though: sometimes for a year, sometimes never, and the facility ends up auctioning the contents for whatever the unpaid balance covers. He said it without much drama, like a fact about weather. I signed for the new key, tested it twice in the new lock just to be sure, and drove home with a bicycle in the trunk that I still, probably, will not get around to selling.
